ACharacterPreviewActor.menu_render_targe.tooltip: Render target for the character screen, where the doll IS the screen and a square 512 was being blown up to full height and reading as mush. Portrait rather than a bigger square: a standing figure in a square frame wastes most of its width, so matching the stage's shape buys resolution the player can see instead of empty background. Every frame is a PNG decoded on the CEF main thread, which is the budget these numbers are traded against. Sized to roughly what the panel actually shows, and no larger. Every pixel here is paid for four times over -- the capture renders it, ReadPixels copies it to the game thread, the scheme handler encodes it to PNG, and CEF decodes it again on the thread that also services the drag -- so this is the single biggest lever on how the character screen feels. It was 1152x1920, which oversampled by half again to buy anti-aliasing; the edges are not worth 2.25x the pixel cost through all four stages. Anti-aliasing has to come out of pixels rather than TemporalAA, which writes an opaque alpha into an LDR capture and puts a black rectangle behind a doll the page composites over its own background. So going BELOW the displayed size costs sharpness twice, and is the wrong direction to economise.

ACharacterPreviewActor.menu_field_of_vie.tooltip: Horizontal field of view for the menu doll at MenuRenderTargetSize's shape. Narrower than the constructor's square-target 55 by exactly the aspect change, so the character frames the same vertically — keeping 55 here would pull the camera back and undo the resolution gain. Only the vertical angle this implies is kept fixed. When the stage is a different shape (see SetMenuStageAspect) the horizontal angle is re-derived for it, because a scene capture's FOV is always the horizontal one.

ACharacterPreviewActor.close_up_distance.tooltip: How far in front of the face the camera sits when framed close, in centimetres. ACharacterPreviewActor.framing_glide_sec.tooltip: Seconds the camera takes to move between the two framings. Fast enough not to be waited on, slow enough that the eye follows the move and keeps track of where the character went.

ACharacterPreviewActor.capture_hertz.tooltip: How often the doll is captured and republished, in frames per second. Each publish reads the render target back on the game thread, which stalls the renderer and copies the entire target — so this is a direct tax on the frame rate of whatever screen is showing the doll. Keep this in step with the rate the page asks at (character.html): capturing faster than the stream buys nothing, and capturing slower makes the stream re-fetch frames it already has. 15 rather than 24 because the doll only ever idles or turns under the player's own drag, and neither reads as choppy at 15.

ACharacterPreviewActor.icon_mannequin_me.tooltip: The shop mannequin the garment icons are modelled on, in the material the enemy itself wears -- so the figure in the icon reads as the same object the player later meets in the dark. Plain SK_LivingMannequin, not the _UE5 variant: it shares 15 of 17 core bones with metahuman_base_skel where the UE5 one shares 14, missing `head` as well as the two spine joints. Both lack spine_04/spine_05, because the mannequin is a UE4-era three-spine hierarchy and MetaHuman is five, so a garment's upper chest falls back to its ref pose. On a still icon that is very likely invisible; if the upper torso drifts, that is the cause.

ACharacterPreviewActor.icon_garment_scal.tooltip: How much room to give a garment over the mannequin, as a uniform scale. The clothes are baked to the MetaHuman body and the mannequin is slightly broader, so without this the two surfaces are near enough coincident that the wood fights through the cloth in patches. Small on purpose: enough to clear the body, not so much that the garment reads as hanging off it.

ACharacterPreviewActor.icon_mannequin_sh.tooltip: How far to shrink the mannequin's skin so the clothes sit over it. The garments carry the exact inverse, so they come out the size they were baked and only the body underneath gets smaller. This is the lever that actually clears the cloth, because the problem is the mannequin's build rather than the garment's fit.

ACharacterPreviewActor.rim_light.tooltip: Behind and above, opposite the key. Without it a turntable character goes to a flat silhouette the moment it turns past three-quarters — the key and fill both sit in front. This is what keeps the back readable and puts an edge on the shoulders and hair against the panel.

ACharacterPreviewActor.bounce_light.tooltip: Low and in front, standing in for bounce off the floor. Lifts the shadow under the chin and brow that a high key alone leaves the face buried in.

With a stockroom behind it that same shot is a character pressed against a wall, so the menu pulls back far enough to put floor under the feet and air above the head.

EnemyMMAnimInstance.search_play_rate.tooltip: How far the motion-matching node may stretch the chosen clip's playback to match actual ground speed. Written onto the node every update, so this is the authority — the value on the ABP's node is ignored. It is owned here because the range that works is a function of the gap between the enemy movement profiles and the speeds the databases were captured at, and both of those are reasoned about in this file. The databases are GASP's, authored on the mannequin at roughly walk 200 / run 500 / sprint 700 cm/s; enemies run 95-364. A walking enemy at 110 therefore needs its walk clip at ~0.55 and a sprinting one can need ~1.6, and anything the interval excludes comes out as feet moving at a different speed from the ground. Min must stay strictly below Max. Equal bounds take a different branch of CalculateWantedPlayRate that ignores speed matching entirely and divides out the trajectory multiplier itself, which would then double up with the stride compensation applied in OnUpdateMotionMatching. This is compensation, not a fix: it stretches clips that were captured at the wrong speed. Stride warping is what removes the mismatch, and no ABP in the project has it.

EnemyMMAnimInstance.stride_reference_pel.tooltip: Pelvis rest height (cm) of the skeleton the locomotion databases were authored on (UEFN mannequin). The trajectory fed to the pose search is speed-scaled by this height over the rig's pelvis height, so bigger rigs select the clips a proportionally slower mannequin would (and vice versa); the motion-matching node plays the pick at PlayRate.Min / multiplier so ground coverage still matches actual velocity.

EnemyMMAnimInstance.stride_speed_multipl.tooltip: Clamp for the size-derived trajectory speed multiplier.

EnemyMMAnimInstance.stair_stride_scale_m.tooltip: Stride scale at full ascent, handed to the anim graph's Stride Warping node. 0.75 means each step covers three quarters of the ground it otherwise would, and playback speeds up by the reciprocal so the enemy still travels at capsule speed — more, smaller steps rather than slower ones. This exists because a stair tread is shorter than a walk stride. The swing foot otherwise sails past several steps and lands somewhere the leg cannot reach, and foot placement then folds the knee through the riser trying to get there. Tuning foot placement only trades that fold against foot contact; the stride is the thing actually at fault.

EnemyMMAnimInstance.stair_full_effect_gr.tooltip: Climb grade (vertical over horizontal speed) at which StairStrideScaleMin is reached. 0.5 is a 27-degree effective slope, which is about a domestic staircase.

EnemyMMAnimInstance.climb_grade_interp_s.tooltip: How fast the measured grade follows reality. Stairs are the reason this is smoothed at all: the capsule climbs them as a series of discrete step-ups separated by flat treads, so the instantaneous grade alternates between a spike and zero several times a second. Averaging it recovers the slope the character is really climbing, and is also why measuring the FLOOR NORMAL would not work here — every tread is flat.

EnemyMMAnimInstance.stair_min_horizontal.tooltip: Horizontal speed below which grade is not measured (divide-by-small-number guard).

CharacterPartDefinition.slot.tooltip: Which slot this fills: Body, Head, Outfit, Hair or Beard.

CharacterPartDefinition.display_name.tooltip: Name shown on the tile in the select screen.

CharacterPartDefinition.body_archetype.tooltip: Body build this part belongs to, or unset for "fits anything". On a Body part this declares the build; on any other part it restricts which builds it can be worn on. Purely a content grouping — nothing branches on it in code beyond FitsArchetype.

CharacterPartDefinition.mesh.tooltip: The skeletal mesh this part puts in its slot. Unset is meaningful for hair and beard, where it is how "None" is authored — the slot is cleared rather than left wearing the previous choice.

CharacterPartDefinition.static_mesh.tooltip: Rigid mesh worn on a bone of the head, for parts that are not skinned. Built hair is exactly this: the groom pipeline emits hair CARDS as a static mesh, not a skeletal one, so a haircut cannot be assigned the way a beard is. Mutually exclusive with Mesh in practice — a part fills its slot with one or the other, and both unset is how "None" is authored.

CharacterPartDefinition.groom.tooltip: Groom this part wears, worn on the same bone as StaticMesh. This is how a built haircut is worn. The groom pipeline bakes hair to cards, but the cards are only half of it — the atlas that gives them their shape is bound by the groom component at draw time, so the same cards mesh hung on a static mesh component renders as a thin scatter of specks. Nothing errors; the hair is simply almost entirely masked away.

CharacterPartDefinition.attach_bone.tooltip: Bone on the head component StaticMesh rides. Unset means the head bone, which is what every haircut wants; it exists so a mod can hang something off a different joint without new code. The mesh is authored in character space, so it is placed with the inverse of the bone's reference-pose transform — attaching it raw would drop the hair at the pelvis and leave it there.

CharacterPartDefinition.attach_reference.tooltip: The body this part was authored against, when that is not the body wearing it. A haircut is baked on one character and worn by all of them, and the two builds do not carry their heads at the same height. Placing it from the WEARER's reference pose therefore drops a hairstyle at whatever height the character it was baked on had, which reads as hair hovering above the skull. Naming the body it was baked on places it against the same skull it was cut for, and it then follows whichever head it is attached to. Unset means the wearer's own body, which is right for anything authored per build.

CharacterPartDefinition.hair_offset.tooltip: Nudge, in centimetres, for the hair worn on THIS head. Z is up; X and Y are the horizontal pair. It is measured in the body mesh's own space rather than the head joint's, because the joint's axes come from the MetaHuman rig and are not the ones anyone writing this by hand would guess -- height is the one that needs tuning in practice, and it is the one that reads as Z. Read from the head part, not the hair part, because that is where the variation is: every haircut is cut on one reference skull and the roster's faces are not that skull, so a fringe that sits right on a broad head rides high on a narrow one. A few millimetres per face is content tuning, and it lives here so it can be dialled in without a rebuild.

CharacterPartDefinition.beard_offset.tooltip: The same nudge, for the facial hair worn on this head. Its own field because a scalp and a jaw are not the same fit and do not miss in the same direction: hair cut for a broad skull rides high on a narrow one, while a beard cut for a heavy jaw stands proud at the sides of a light one. Sharing one number meant dropping a fringe onto the brow also dropped the beard off the chin.

CharacterPartDefinition.mesh_scale.tooltip: Uniform scale for the whole figure, set on the body part. The two builds were sculpted at their own heights and the shorter stands most of a head under the other. Every haircut and beard is cut on one reference skull, so on the smaller head they all read a size too big -- evening the heights out fixes the fit as well as the height. Uniform on purpose. Stretching only the vertical would make a tall thin caricature of a body someone modelled; growing all three keeps the figure and only changes how much room it takes up. Everything else the character wears hangs off the body component, so face, hair, beard and clothes come with it.

CharacterPartDefinition.materials.tooltip: Material overrides for the mesh this part puts in its slot, keyed by the mesh's own material slot name. Keyed rather than indexed because the two body builds wear differently cut garments whose slots are in no dependable order — an outfit look is the same pair of meshes wearing a different pair of instances, and matching those by index is how a shirt finish ends up on the shorts.

CharacterPartDefinition.visible_material.tooltip: Material slots on this part's mesh to DRAW, with everything else on it hidden. Empty means draw the whole mesh, which is what every part outside the Top and Bottom slots wants. This is how one garment mesh fills two slots. A bought outfit arrives as a single mesh -- sweater, belt, trousers and boots in one -- and the MetaHuman pipeline will not cut it: its Top Garment and Bottom Garment slots accept the outfit and then bake the whole of it into both, so the halves cannot come from the build. What the bake DOES preserve is one material slot per garment piece, so naming the pieces is enough to show half a mesh and hide the rest. Six outfits therefore become six tops and six bottoms that mix freely, from the same twelve meshes and no extra content. The cost is memory: each half still carries the other's geometry, hidden. Nothing is drawn for it. Names must match the mesh's own material slot names exactly. One that matches nothing warns rather than failing, because the alternative is a garment that silently renders as nothing at all.

CharacterPartDefinition.b_hides_hair.tooltip: Whether wearing this part clears the Hair slot. Headwear needs it. A cap in these packs is modelled on a bare scalp, so worn over a haircut it does not sit on the hair -- the hair grows through it. Hiding the hair is wrong in a different way (a cap should show hair at the back) but it is the wrong that reads as a choice rather than as a broken mesh. A flag on the part rather than a rule about the slot, so a hat modelled with room for hair can simply not set it.

CharacterPartDefinition.hides_hair.tooltip: Whether wearing this part clears the Hair slot. Headwear needs it. A cap in these packs is modelled on a bare scalp, so worn over a haircut it does not sit on the hair -- the hair grows through it. Hiding the hair is wrong in a different way (a cap should show hair at the back) but it is the wrong that reads as a choice rather than as a broken mesh. A flag on the part rather than a rule about the slot, so a hat modelled with room for hair can simply not set it.

CharacterPartDefinition.body_materials.tooltip: Materials this part puts on the BODY, keyed the same way. Only a head uses it, and it exists because complexion belongs to the face rather than to the build. A body mesh ships baked skin textures of whoever it was built from, so a head worn on the shared build arrives with a different complexion from the neck down — one character, two skin tones, and nothing in the logs about it. The head therefore carries its own body skin and repaints the build it is worn on.

CharacterPartDefinition.thumbnail.tooltip: Tile image for the select screen, as a URL the WebUI can fetch -- the mod's own web folder is served, so "/img/parts/.png" is the whole of it. Not a texture asset: these are rendered from the parts themselves and consumed only by an tag, so importing 150 of them into the content tree would buy nothing but cook time.

CharacterPartDefinition.swatch.tooltip: Flat colour this part shows as in the picker, as "#rrggbb". A colour is the one thing a rendered tile is worse at showing than a square of the colour itself: ten heads of hair photographed under the same lamp differ by less than the lighting does. Authored rather than sampled from the material, because what belongs on the swatch is what the hair reads as in the world, not the melanin value that produces it.

CharacterPartDefinition.fabric.tooltip: Garment this part is a colourway of, for the slots that come in colours. The wardrobe is authored as one definition per cut per colour, because that is what the material pairs actually are -- but showing forty tiles that are five garments eight times over is not a wardrobe, it is a paint chart. The screen folds a fabric's colours into one tile and a row of swatches; this is what tells it which tiles are the same garment. Unset means the part stands alone: a preset look that comes in one finish is still its own tile with no swatch row.

CharacterPartDefinition.preview_anim_blu.tooltip: Animation blueprint the character-select preview runs, so the doll idles and breathes instead of standing in reference pose. Read from the Body part only, because the body owns the skeleton the blueprint is built against. Only the preview uses this — the live pawn's animation comes from its own Blueprint. It lives on the definition rather than being hardcoded so a mod shipping its own rig can supply a matching one.

CharacterPartDefinition.preview_idle_ani.tooltip: Looping idle the preview plays when there is no animation blueprint. Read from the Body part, for the same reason the blueprint is. A doll standing in reference pose reads as a bug rather than as a character, and a single looping sequence is the whole of what a turntable needs — the blueprint above is for a rig that wants blending or state, not for this. Whichever is set wins, blueprint first.

CharacterPartDefinition.sort_order.tooltip: Ascending display order within the slot; ties break on id.

ScpCharacterAppearance.top_id.tooltip: Upper garment, and lower garment. Two fields rather than one OutfitId because clothing is two choices. A bought outfit is one mesh covering the whole body, so it used to be one pick and six looks; the same meshes split by material slot give a top and a bottom that mix freely, which is thirty-six. See UCharacterPartDefinition::VisibleMaterialSlots for how one mesh fills both slots.

ScpCharacterAppearance.shoes_id.tooltip: Footwear and headwear, both of which used to arrive welded to a garment. Their own slots because shoes were coming along with the trousers -- pick the cargo shorts and you got trainers, pick a fabric recolour and you got bare feet, on the same character. Same mesh-sharing trick as the top and bottom: a shoe part is a whole-outfit mesh with only its footwear material drawn.

ScpCharacterAppearance.beard_color_id.tooltip: Beard colour, or the part that means "whatever the hair is". Its own field rather than a reuse of HairColorId because the two are not the same choice: a man greys at the chin first. The roster's default is the match-hair part, so a player who never opens the picker never has to think about it and never ends up with a beard that does not belong to him.

ScpCharacterAppearance.hair_tint.tooltip: The colour behind the colour wheel, for hair and for facial hair. A dyed head is still a part id -- the "Custom" swatch, which names the dyeable material -- and this is what that part is dyed to. Two fields, matching the two pickers, and both ignored while a named colour is worn. Kept rather than reset when the player moves back to a named colour, so returning to the wheel returns to the shade they mixed.

EnemyDefinition.b_invulnerable.tooltip: An invulnerable enemy carries Status.Buff.Invulnerable from spawn: the health set zeroes every damage application, so it can never be wounded, staggered, or killed.

EnemyDefinition.invulnerable.tooltip: An invulnerable enemy carries Status.Buff.Invulnerable from spawn: the health set zeroes every damage application, so it can never be wounded, staggered, or killed.

EnemyDefinition.variants.tooltip: Easy/Medium/Hard re-skin data. Base is intentionally absent (see EEnemyDifficultyVariantTier).

EnemyDefinition.shirt_material_slot_inde.tooltip: Material slot on the enemy's skeletal mesh that receives the variant tint MID. INDEX_NONE = no shirt slot on this enemy.

EnemySpawnScalingDefinition.enemies_per_.tooltip: Enemies each spawn point places, indexed by player count - 1. Fractional values are real: the whole part is guaranteed and the remainder is a per-point probability, so 1.5 means half the store's spawn points place a pair. Averaging across the many points in a store is what makes a fraction meaningful; rounding would quantise the whole world to +0% or +100%.

EnemySpawnScalingDefinition.player_exclu.tooltip: Multiplier on FEnemySpawnParams::MinDistanceToAnyPlayer, indexed by player count - 1. The exclusion radius is per-player by design — every player deserves the same "nothing pops in next to me" guarantee — but the tested area is the UNION of those discs, so a spread-out lobby suppresses spawning rather than increasing it. Shrinking the radius as players are added holds the excluded area roughly constant (1/sqrt(N)).

EnemySpawnScalingDefinition.pack_min_dis.tooltip: MinDistanceToAnyEnemy used for the SECOND and later enemy at one spawn point. The authored value spreads population across the store (6000 for a BoneHead), which would reject every companion before it was placed. A deliberate pack does not want that rule — only enough room not to stand inside each other. HasRoomForEnemy still has the final say on overlap.

EnemySpawnScalingDefinition.planned_min_.tooltip: Player-exclusion radius used by a spawn point that was APPROVED while its tile was still generating (URandomEnemySpawnerComponent's spawn plans). Replaces the authored FEnemySpawnParams::MinDistanceToAnyPlayer for that one placement, and only ever downward. A point cannot place anything until its tile has finished generating, and a player walking toward that tile has closed most of the distance by then — so re-testing the authored radius at placement time refuses the point it already approved, and the store ahead of a moving player stays empty. Worse, the authored 5000 barely overlaps the region that HAS a navmesh: navigation is generated only around invokers (UNavigationInvokerComponent defaults, 3000 generation / 5000 removal), so beyond ~5000 from a player there is usually nothing to project a spawn location onto. What survives is a pop-in floor: far enough that nothing materialises in somebody's face, near enough to be inside the navmesh that actually exists.

EnemyDifficultyTier.enemies_can_spawn.tooltip: Enemies that can spawn from this tier (one selected by weight).

EnemySpawnPointDefinition.enemies_by_dif.tooltip: Enemies grouped by tile difficulty tier. Lookup is floor-based: tile picks the largest key <= tile difficulty.

ComputerTerminalDefinition.terminal_tier.tooltip: Hardware generation: 1 = green CRT text shell, 2 = windowed GUI, 3 = SCiPnet restricted access.

ComputerTerminalDefinition.auto_run_prog.tooltip: Program id to launch as soon as the shell finishes booting. Empty = drop the operator at the launcher.

ComputerTerminalDefinition.unlocked_prog.tooltip: Program ids installed on this machine. Empty means "everything shipped in web/programs that this tier can run" — the sane default for set dressing, so a new program appears on every terminal without touching each definition.

DamageableFurnitureDefinition.b_is_damag.tooltip: Whether this furniture can be damaged at all. False makes it scenery: every damage gameplay effect is refused at UScpHealthSet::PostGameplayEffectExecute (so hazards and decay are covered, not only melee), AI2 never selects it as something to smash, and it stays a solid nav blocker instead of a breakable health bucket. The flag exists because interactable is a SUBSET of damageable here — every interactable class descends from this one — so wiring a prop up to a screen used to hand players something to break. ScpCharacterMovementComponent.b_enable_s.tooltip: Scale max speed down when climbing, so a pawn crosses a staircase at a believable pace instead of a flat-ground one. This is the movement half of the stair work. Shortening the animation stride alone cannot slow anything down: ground speed is fixed by this component, so the stride scale has to be paid for with a reciprocal play rate, and the enemy scurries up the steps at full walking speed. Scaling speed by the SAME factor as the stride leaves the cadence alone — short steps at a normal rate, which is what walking slowly is. Off by default so it stays an enemy behaviour; AScpEnemyCharacter opts in. Turning it on for players changes how the game feels to move in and is a deliberate choice.

ScpCharacterMovementComponent.enable_slo.tooltip: Scale max speed down when climbing, so a pawn crosses a staircase at a believable pace instead of a flat-ground one. This is the movement half of the stair work. Shortening the animation stride alone cannot slow anything down: ground speed is fixed by this component, so the stride scale has to be paid for with a reciprocal play rate, and the enemy scurries up the steps at full walking speed. Scaling speed by the SAME factor as the stride leaves the cadence alone — short steps at a normal rate, which is what walking slowly is. Off by default so it stays an enemy behaviour; AScpEnemyCharacter opts in. Turning it on for players changes how the game feels to move in and is a deliberate choice.

ScpCharacterMovementComponent.slope_asce.tooltip: Speed multiplier at full ascent. 0.5 means half flat-ground speed up a staircase. Setting this EQUAL to the anim instance's StairStrideScaleMin is mathematically the tidiest answer -- the two cancel in GetStairPlayRateMultiplier and leg cadence is left completely untouched. It was tried at 0.3/0.3 on 2026-08-19 and does not work: the enemy stops stepping and glides up the stairs instead. There is a floor on how slowly a motion-matched enemy can walk, and it is well above zero. GASP's locomotion is authored on the mannequin at roughly walk 200 cm/s, enemy walk profiles are around 110, and SearchPlayRate bottoms out at 0.5. Take a third of 110 and the pose search is being asked for a trajectory barely distinguishable from standing still, so it returns idles -- which is exactly what gliding is. Slowing an enemy is therefore bounded by what the databases can represent, not by taste. So this deliberately does NOT match the stride scale: some cadence increase is the price of staying inside the range the databases cover. If it ever wants lowering, the enemy walk profile has to come up to meet it, or the locomotion set needs clips authored slower.

ScpCharacterMovementComponent.slope_desc.tooltip: Speed multiplier at full descent. 1 (no slowdown) by default: descending already looks right, and slowing it is a separate judgement from fixing the climb.

ScpCharacterMovementComponent.slope_full.tooltip: Climb grade at which the min scales are reached. Keep this in step with the anim instance's StairFullEffectGrade — if the two curves disagree, the speed scale and the stride scale disagree, and the difference comes out as foot sliding.

ScpCharacterMovementComponent.climb_grad.tooltip: How fast the measured grade follows reality. Smoothing is not optional on stairs: the capsule climbs them as discrete step-ups separated by flat treads, so the instantaneous grade alternates between a spike and zero several times a second. This is also why the grade is measured from capsule height over time rather than from the floor normal — every tread is flat, so the normal reads level all the way up.

ScpCharacterMovementComponent.slope_min_.tooltip: Horizontal speed below which grade is not measured (divide-by-small-number guard).
